label: Denial of Right to Contact Attorney or Relative/Friend Before Deciding Whether to Take a Breath Test (Copelin/Zsupnik)
motion_heading: The Breath Test Must Be Suppressed Because the Defendant Was Denied the Statutory Right to Consult Before Deciding Whether to Submit to a Breath Test

review_conditions.display_note: Whether a lack of privacy violates AS 12.25.150(b) is a reasonableness balancing test, not a bright-line rule — gather the specific circumstances (what could be overheard, whether it actually inhibited communication) before relying on this issue as written.
Whether the time allowed was 'reasonable' is fact-specific. Document exactly how much time was requested and needed versus actually given.

excluded_explanations.display_note: The request to contact a relative/friend appears to have served a purely personal purpose, not a defense-related one. Alaska's supreme court has expressly left open whether denial of a non-defense-related request requires suppression (Zsupnik v. State, 789 P.2d 357, 361 n.4 (Alaska 1990)), and Winfrey v. State, 78 P.3d 725 (Alaska App. 2003), has declined to extend suppression to non-defense-related requests. This may still be worth raising in the alternative depending on the full record, but it isn't clearly supported by current law.

It's unclear whether the request to contact a relative/friend served a defense-related purpose. Under Zsupnik v. State, 789 P.2d 357 (Alaska 1990), that purpose determines whether suppression is available — developing this fact (what your client said the reason was) could make this issue viable.

rule_statements.text: A person has the right to telephone or otherwise communicate with an attorney and any relative or friend immediately after arrest.

This right requires police to give a person arrested for driving under the influence a reasonable opportunity to contact an attorney by phone before being required to decide whether to submit to a breath test, and violation of this right requires suppression of the test results.
This right extends to requests to contact a relative or friend when the request served a purpose related to the defense process such as obtaining advice on whether to take the test.
Police must make a reasonable effort to allow the arrested person to communicate privately.
The right is not absolute and does not permit indefinite delay; what counts as a reasonable opportunity is balanced against the state's need to administer the test in a timely manner.

_author_notes: private_communication is new wording for Farrell's proposition (previously summarized as 'police must make reasonable effort to accommodate private consultation'). Verify against the opinion.
